Before you start

First you\'ll hear a few chords played one after another. A chord is several notes sounding together. Their job is to set up a \"home\" note — the one everything else gets compared to. The last chord lands back on home, so home is the sound you\'re left with.
Then, after a short gap, you\'ll hear one single note on its own.
That single note is the question. Your job is to say where it sits compared to home.

You answer with the buttons at the bottom. Right now there are three: \"1\" is home itself, and \"3\" and \"5\" are the two other notes from that opening chord — a little above home, and higher still.

You won\'t always be sure, and that\'s expected. Guessing is how this gets easier — nothing is scored and nothing is held against you.

Major

Something new: major or minor
Up to now you\'ve been naming single notes inside one key. This asks something different, and simpler: you just say which of two flavors the whole thing has.
Every key comes in one of two flavors, called major and minor. Same set of steps, one of them shifted slightly, and that one shift changes the whole character of the sound.
You\'ll hear a short passage. Your job: major, or minor. That\'s the whole question — no notes to name, two buttons.
Most people hear this before they can explain it. Don\'t look for a rule; play the two examples below a few times and let the difference land on its own.
Hear them side by side
Play the major one
Play the minor one
Play each a few times, and switch between them. The contrast is much easier to hear than either one alone.
You won\'t be sure at first, and guessing is fine. Nothing here is scored against you.
Start
What am I listening for?
Something new: minor
Everything works the same way as before. Chords set up a \"home\" note, then one note plays, and you say where it sits. What changes is the flavor of the scale those notes come from.

Play the example and you\'ll hear it straight away. Minor sounds darker, heavier, sadder — most people hear the difference long before they can name it. You don\'t need a word for it. You just need to hear where the note sits.
One button looks different now: \u266d3, said \"flat three\". It sits between 2 and 3 — a little lower than the 3 you already know. That small drop is most of what makes the whole thing sound minor.

It keeps its number because it is still the third note of the scale. The \u266d just says \"the lower version of it\". Same for \u266d6 later on. A number always means the same distance from home, in every key and either flavor — that is the point of the labels.
Start practicing
How minor works
Notes between the notes

Until now every note you\'ve named came from the seven the key is built on. Those seven were never all the notes there are — they\'re the ones this key uses as its own. In between some of them sits another note, closer to its neighbor than any two of the seven are to each other. You\'ve been hearing these in music your whole life. Now you get to name them.

A new note needs a name, and it borrows one. \u266f4 means \"the 4 you know, nudged up\". \u266d7 means \"the 7 you know, nudged down\". The number still says the same thing it always did — how far from home — and the sign in front says which version of it you\'re hearing. Exactly like \u266d3 in minor.

On the ladder these sit alongside the note they\'re named after, slightly narrower, so you can see at a glance which is which. \u266f4 is beside 4, just above it, and below the 5 it wants to fall into.

You get one of these at a time, mixed in with all the notes you already know — that\'s the point. On its own a new note is just a sound. What makes it recognizable is where it sits against the ones around it.
Start practicing
Something new: you won\'t be told which

You\'ve been naming notes in major, and naming notes in minor, always knowing which one you were in. From here you won\'t be told. Each round picks one or the other, and the chords at the start are the only thing that says which.

That\'s why there are more buttons now. All ten are on screen every round — the ones you know from major and the ones you know from minor, side by side. They don\'t change between rounds, because if they did, they\'d be giving the answer away before you\'d heard anything.

So it\'s two things at once, in order. Listen to the chords and let the flavor land — bright or dark. Then place the note against that. Most of the work is the first step, and you\'ve already done it on its own.
Try one
Play this and decide the flavor before you think about the note at all.
Which was it?
That one was minor, and the note was %1$s. In major the same button position would have been a different note — which is exactly why the flavor has to come first.
After every answer you\'ll be told which flavor it was, right or wrong. That way a miss tells you something: whether you placed the note wrong, or heard the key wrong.

Something new: hear it before it plays

Every exercise so far played a note and asked you to name it. This one runs backwards. We name the note first, then there\'s silence, and your job during that silence is to hear the note in your head. Then it plays, and you say whether it was the one you were holding.

The chords set up home, the same as always. A number appears — say it\'s 5. Nothing plays. You find the 5 in your head and hold onto it. Then a note sounds. Was that your 5, or was it lower, or higher?
The silence is not the app loading. It is the exercise. Nothing is timing you and nothing is watching how fast you get there — take the whole gap.

If "hear it in your head" sounds like something you can\'t do, try this: think of a song you know and let the first line play internally, without singing. That is the thing. It is the same skill, aimed at one note.
Try one
The example holds %1$s. Play it, hold that note through the silence, and see whether the note that arrives is the one you had.
Play the example
What was it?
That was a match — the note that played was exactly the %1$s you were holding.
That was not a match — the note that played was %1$s the %2$s you were holding.
lower than
higher than
Three buttons: it matched, it was lower, or it was higher. Early on, spotting that something was off at all is the win — you won\'t be marked down for getting the direction wrong.

Answering by singing
You can sing your answer instead of tapping it. Everything else stays the same: you hear the setup, then the note, then you answer.
Sing it high or low, whichever is comfortable for your voice. It counts either way.
For example
Say the answer is 3, and you sing it slightly flat. That still counts as 3. The app works out which note you were going for, and close is close enough.
How well you sing is not part of this. Nothing here scores your voice.
If the app cannot make out what you sang, it simply asks again. That is never counted as a wrong answer.
The buttons are always there too. You can tap any question instead, at any time.
